questions.q: Given \(f(x)=\sqrt{x+4}\) and \(g(x)=x^2-4\), find \((f\circ g)(2)\) and state the domain restriction that makes \(f\circ g\) defined.
questions.answer: \((f\circ g)(2)=f(g(2))=f(0)=\sqrt{0+4}=2\). In general, \(f\circ g\) requires \(g(x)+4\geq0\), i.e. \(x^2\geq0\), which holds for all real \(x\) — so \(f\circ g\) is defined everywhere.
questions.explanation: \((f\circ g)(2)=f(g(2))=f(0)=\sqrt{0+4}=2\). In general, \(f\circ g\) requires \(g(x)+4\geq0\), i.e. \(x^2\geq0\), which holds for all real \(x\) — so \(f\circ g\) is defined everywhere.

questions.q: Write \(h(x)=(3x-5)^4\) as a composition \(h(x)=f(g(x))\) for two simpler functions \(f\) and \(g\).
questions.answer: Let \(g(x)=3x-5\) (inner function) and \(f(x)=x^4\) (outer function). Then \(f(g(x))=(3x-5)^4=h(x)\).
questions.explanation: Let \(g(x)=3x-5\) (inner function) and \(f(x)=x^4\) (outer function). Then \(f(g(x))=(3x-5)^4=h(x)\).

questions.q: Write \(h(x)=\sqrt{x^2+1}\) as a composition of two functions.
questions.answer: Let \(g(x)=x^2+1\) and \(f(x)=\sqrt{x}\). Then \(f(g(x))=\sqrt{x^2+1}=h(x)\).
questions.explanation: Let \(g(x)=x^2+1\) and \(f(x)=\sqrt{x}\). Then \(f(g(x))=\sqrt{x^2+1}=h(x)\).

questions.q: Verify algebraically that \(f(x)=\frac{x-2}{3}\) and \(g(x)=3x+2\) are inverses of each other.
questions.answer: \(f(g(x))=\frac{(3x+2)-2}{3}=\frac{3x}{3}=x\). \(g(f(x))=3\left(\frac{x-2}{3}\right)+2=(x-2)+2=x\). Since both compositions return \(x\), \(f\) and \(g\) are inverses.
questions.explanation: \(f(g(x))=\frac{(3x+2)-2}{3}=\frac{3x}{3}=x\). \(g(f(x))=3\left(\frac{x-2}{3}\right)+2=(x-2)+2=x\). Since both compositions return \(x\), \(f\) and \(g\) are inverses.

questions.q: Find the inverse of \(f(x)=2x^3+1\), and verify that \(f(f^{-1}(x))=x\) for one value, say \(x=17\).
The graph shows \(f(x)=x^2\) (restricted to \(x\geq0\)) and its inverse \(f^{-1}(x)=\sqrt{x}\), which are reflections of each other across the line \(y=x\).
parts: State the domain restriction placed on \(f(x)=x^2\) needed for it to have an inverse, and explain why.
Confirm from the graph that \(f\) and \(f^{-1}\) intersect on the line \(y=x\), and find that intersection point algebraically.
answers: \(f(x)=x^2\) must be restricted to \(x\geq0\) (or \(x\leq0\)) because the full parabola fails the horizontal line test — without restricting the domain, \(f\) is not one-to-one and has no inverse function.
Setting \(f(x)=x\): \(x^2=x\), so \(x^2-x=0\), \(x(x-1)=0\), giving \(x=0\) or \(x=1\). Both points \((0,0)\) and \((1,1)\) lie on \(y=x\), matching where the two curves cross in the graph.

questions.q: Given \(f(x)=\frac{1}{x-3}\) and \(g(x)=x+1\), find the domain of \((f\circ g)(x)\).
questions.target: Domain and range of composite and inverse functions
questions.answer: \((f\circ g)(x)=f(x+1)=\frac{1}{(x+1)-3}=\frac{1}{x-2}\). This is undefined at \(x=2\), so the domain is all reals except \(x=2\).
questions.explanation: \((f\circ g)(x)=f(x+1)=\frac{1}{(x+1)-3}=\frac{1}{x-2}\). This is undefined at \(x=2\), so the domain is all reals except \(x=2\).

questions.q: A temperature-conversion function \(C(F)=\frac{5}{9}(F-32)\) converts Fahrenheit to Celsius. Find \(C^{-1}(F)\) and interpret what it computes.
questions.target: Applying composite and inverse functions in context
questions.answer: Solve \(C=\frac{5}{9}(F-32)\) for \(F\): \(\frac{9C}{5}=F-32\), so \(F=\frac{9}{5}C+32\). This is \(C^{-1}\), which converts a Celsius temperature back to Fahrenheit.
questions.explanation: Solve \(C=\frac{5}{9}(F-32)\) for \(F\): \(\frac{9C}{5}=F-32\), so \(F=\frac{9}{5}C+32\). This is \(C^{-1}\), which converts a Celsius temperature back to Fahrenheit.

questions.q: Determine whether \(f(x)=x^3-4x\) has an inverse function over its entire domain. Justify using the horizontal line test.
questions.answer: Since \(f(x)=x^3-4x\) has multiple turning points (a cubic with two real critical points), a horizontal line such as \(y=0\) intersects the graph at more than one point (\(x=0,\pm2\)), failing the horizontal line test. So \(f\) does not have an inverse function over its entire domain.
questions.explanation: Since \(f(x)=x^3-4x\) has multiple turning points (a cubic with two real critical points), a horizontal line such as \(y=0\) intersects the graph at more than one point (\(x=0,\pm2\)), failing the horizontal line test. So \(f\) does not have an inverse function over its entire domain.

questions.q: Explain why \(f(x)=5x-2\) passes the horizontal line test for all real \(x\), and find its inverse.
questions.answer: \(f(x)=5x-2\) is a line with nonzero slope, so it is strictly increasing and every horizontal line crosses it exactly once — it passes the horizontal line test everywhere. Solving \(y=5x-2\) for \(x\): \(f^{-1}(x)=\frac{x+2}{5}\).
questions.explanation: \(f(x)=5x-2\) is a line with nonzero slope, so it is strictly increasing and every horizontal line crosses it exactly once — it passes the horizontal line test everywhere. Solving \(y=5x-2\) for \(x\): \(f^{-1}(x)=\frac{x+2}{5}\).

questions.q: Given \(f(x)=\frac{1}{x}\) and \(g(x)=x-4\), find \((f\circ g)(x)\) and state its domain.
questions.answer: \((f\circ g)(x)=f(x-4)=\frac{1}{x-4}\). This is undefined at \(x=4\), so the domain is all reals except \(x=4\).
questions.explanation: \((f\circ g)(x)=f(x-4)=\frac{1}{x-4}\). This is undefined at \(x=4\), so the domain is all reals except \(x=4\).

questions.q: Find the inverse function of \(f(x)=\frac{2x-1}{x+3}\).
questions.target: Domain and range of composite and inverse functions
questions.answer: Step 1: Set \(y = \frac{2x - 1}{x + 3}\) and swap variables \(x\) and \(y\): \(x = \frac{2y - 1}{y + 3}\) Step 2: Multiply both sides by \((y + 3)\): \(x(y + 3) = 2y - 1 \Rightarrow xy + 3x = 2y - 1\) Step 3: Group terms containing \(y\) on one side: \(xy - 2y = -3x - 1 \Rightarrow y(x - 2) = -(3x + 1)\) Step 4: Solve for \(y\): \(y = \mathbf{\frac{-3x - 1}{x - 2}} = \mathbf{\frac{3x + 1}{2 - x}} \quad (x eq 2)\)
questions.explanation: Step 1: Set \(y = \frac{2x - 1}{x + 3}\) and swap variables \(x\) and \(y\): \(x = \frac{2y - 1}{y + 3}\) Step 2: Multiply both sides by \((y + 3)\): \(x(y + 3) = 2y - 1 \Rightarrow xy + 3x = 2y - 1\) Step 3: Group terms containing \(y\) on one side: \(xy - 2y = -3x - 1 \Rightarrow y(x - 2) = -(3x + 1)\) Step 4: Solve for \(y\): \(y = \mathbf{\frac{-3x - 1}{x - 2}} = \mathbf{\frac{3x + 1}{2 - x}} \quad (x eq 2)\)

questions.q: Determine whether the function \(g(x) = \frac{x^3}{x^2 + 4}\) is even, odd, or neither.
questions.target: Applying composite and inverse functions in context
questions.answer: Evaluate \(g(-x)\) by substituting \(-x\) for every occurrence of \(x\): \(g(-x) = \frac{(-x)^3}{(-x)^2 + 4} = \frac{-x^3}{x^2 + 4} = -\left(\frac{x^3}{x^2 + 4}\right) = -g(x)\) Because \(g(-x) = -g(x)\) for all \(x \in \mathbb{R}\), \(g(x)\) is an odd function (symmetric with respect to \(180^\circ\) rotation about the origin).
questions.explanation: Evaluate \(g(-x)\) by substituting \(-x\) for every occurrence of \(x\): \(g(-x) = \frac{(-x)^3}{(-x)^2 + 4} = \frac{-x^3}{x^2 + 4} = -\left(\frac{x^3}{x^2 + 4}\right) = -g(x)\) Because \(g(-x) = -g(x)\) for all \(x \in \mathbb{R}\), \(g(x)\) is an odd function (symmetric with respect to \(180^\circ\) rotation about the origin).

questions.q: A function is defined piecewise: \(f(x) = x^2\) for \(x < 0\), and \(f(x) = 2x+1\) for \(x \geq 0\). What is the value of \(f(-3) + f(2)\)?
questions.answer: Evaluate each term according to its interval condition: For \(x = -3 < 0\): \(f(-3) = (-3)^2 = 9\). For \(x = 2 \geq 0\): \(f(2) = 2(2) + 1 = 5\). Sum: \(f(-3) + f(2) = 9 + 5 = \mathbf{14}\).
questions.explanation: Evaluate each term according to its interval condition: For \(x = -3 < 0\): \(f(-3) = (-3)^2 = 9\). For \(x = 2 \geq 0\): \(f(2) = 2(2) + 1 = 5\). Sum: \(f(-3) + f(2) = 9 + 5 = \mathbf{14}\).

questions.q: Let \(f(x) = \frac{2x^2 - 8}{x^2 - x - 6}\). (a) Find all vertical asymptotes. (b) Find the horizontal asymptote. (c) Find all x-intercepts.
questions.answer: (a) Factor denominator: (x-3)(x+2); factor numerator: 2(x-2)(x+2). The (x+2) factor cancels, so x=-2 is a hole, not a vertical asymptote. Vertical asymptote: x=3 only. (b) Degrees equal; leading ratio = 2/1 = 2. Horizontal asymptote: y=2. (c) Factor numerator: 2(x²-4) = 2(x-2)(x+2). x-intercept where 2(x-2)(x+2)=0 and denominator ≠ 0: x=2 (x=-2 is a hole, not intercept).
questions.explanation: (a) Factor denominator: (x-3)(x+2); factor numerator: 2(x-2)(x+2). The (x+2) factor cancels, so x=-2 is a hole, not a vertical asymptote. Vertical asymptote: x=3 only. (b) Degrees equal; leading ratio = 2/1 = 2. Horizontal asymptote: y=2. (c) Factor numerator: 2(x²-4) = 2(x-2)(x+2). x-intercept where 2(x-2)(x+2)=0 and denominator ≠ 0: x=2 (x=-2 is a hole, not intercept).

questions.q: Consider the function \(f(x) = 2x + 5\). Which of the following represents the inverse function \(f^{-1}(x)\)?
questions.target: Applying composite and inverse functions in context
questions.answer: To find the inverse function \(f^{-1}(x)\), we first replace \(f(x)\) with \(y\): \(y = 2x + 5\). Next, we swap \(x\) and \(y\): \(x = 2y + 5\). Now, we solve for \(y\) to isolate the inverse function. Subtract 5 from both sides: \(x - 5 = 2y\). Divide both sides by 2: \(\frac{x-5}{2} = y\). Therefore, the inverse function is \(f^{-1}(x) = \frac{x-5}{2}\).
questions.explanation: To find the inverse function \(f^{-1}(x)\), we first replace \(f(x)\) with \(y\): \(y = 2x + 5\). Next, we swap \(x\) and \(y\): \(x = 2y + 5\). Now, we solve for \(y\) to isolate the inverse function. Subtract 5 from both sides: \(x - 5 = 2y\). Divide both sides by 2: \(\frac{x-5}{2} = y\). Therefore, the inverse function is \(f^{-1}(x) = \frac{x-5}{2}\).

questions.q: Find the inverse of \(f(x)=\frac{3x+2}{x-1}\) and state its domain.
questions.answer: Swap: \(x=\frac{3y+2}{y-1}\Rightarrow x(y-1)=3y+2\Rightarrow xy-x=3y+2\Rightarrow y(x-3)=x+2\Rightarrow y=\frac{x+2}{x-3}\).
questions.explanation: Swap: \(x=\frac{3y+2}{y-1}\Rightarrow x(y-1)=3y+2\Rightarrow xy-x=3y+2\Rightarrow y(x-3)=x+2\Rightarrow y=\frac{x+2}{x-3}\).

questions.q: The graph of a polynomial function \(f(x)\) of degree 4 is shown in the figure below. The graph is tangent to the \(x\)-axis at \((-2, 0)\), intersects the \(x\)-axis at \((1, 0)\) and \((3, 0)\), and crosses the \(y\)-axis at \((0, -6)\). A new polynomial \(Q(x)\) is defined by \(Q(x) = f(x) + \frac{1}{2}x^3.\) When \(Q(x)\) is divided by \(x^2 - 4\), the remainder is the linear polynomial \(R(x)\). What is the value of \(R(5)\)?
questions.answer: We solve the problem in two key phases: identifying the polynomial \(f(x)\) from its graphical features, and applying the Polynomial Remainder Theorem to determine \(R(x)\). **Step 1: Determine \(f(x)\)** - Because the graph is tangent to the \(x\)-axis at \(x = -2\), \((x + 2)\) is a factor with an even multiplicity of at least \(2\). - Because the graph crosses the \(x\)-axis at \(x = 1\) and \(x = 3\), \((x - 1)\) and \((x - 3)\) are factors with odd multiplicities of at least \(1\). - Since \(f(x)\) is of degree 4, the sum of multiplicities must equal 4. Therefore, the multiplicity of \((x + 2)\) is 2, and the multiplicities of \((x - 1)\) and \((x - 3)\) are each 1: \(f(x) = a(x + 2)^2(x - 1)(x - 3)\) Using the \(y\)-intercept \((0, -6)\): \(f(0) = a(0 + 2)^2(0 - 1)(0 - 3) = a(4)(-1)(-3) = 12a = -6 \Rightarrow a = -\frac{1}{2}\) Thus, \(f(x) = -\frac{1}{2}(x + 2)^2(x - 1)(x - 3).\) **Step 2: Apply the Division Algorithm** When \(Q(x)\) is divided by the quadratic divisor \(x^2 - 4 = (x - 2)(x + 2)\), the remainder \(R(x)\) has degree at most 1, so \(R(x) = mx + b\). By the division algorithm: \(Q(x) = (x^2 - 4)q(x) + (mx + b)\) Evaluating at the roots of the divisor, \(x = 2\) and \(x = -2\): \(Q(2) = 2m + b\) \(Q(-2) = -2m + b\) **Step 3: Compute \(Q(2)\) and \(Q(-2)\)** Using \(Q(x) = f(x) + \frac{1}{2}x^3\): - At \(x = 2\): \(f(2) = -\frac{1}{2}(2 + 2)^2(2 - 1)(2 - 3) = -\frac{1}{2}(16)(1)(-1) = 8\) \(Q(2) = f(2) + \frac{1}{2}(2)^3 = 8 + 4 = 12\) - At \(x = -2\): \(f(-2) = 0\) \(Q(-2) = 0 + \frac{1}{2}(-2)^3 = -4\) **Step 4: Solve for \(m\), \(b\), and evaluate \(R(5)\)** We have the system: \(\left\{ 2m + b = 12 ; -2m + b = -4 \right.\) Adding the two equations yields \(2b = 8 \Rightarrow b = 4\). Subtracting the second equation from the first yields \(4m = 16 \Rightarrow m = 4\). Therefore, the remainder polynomial is: \(R(x) = 4x + 4\) Evaluating at \(x = 5\): \(R(5) = 4(5) + 4 = 24.\) **Distractor Analysis:** - Choice B (\(18\)) arises from a sign error when computing \((-2)^3\), giving \(Q(-2) = 4\), which leads to \(R(x) = 2x + 8\) and \(R(5) = 18\). - Choice C (\(17\)) results from treating \(x = -2\) as a root of multiplicity 1 instead of 2 (assuming degree 3), giving \(f(x) = -(x+2)(x-1)(x-3)\), which leads to \(R(x) = 3x + 2\) and \(R(5) = 17\). - Choice D (\(14\)) results from finding the remainder of \(f(x)\) divided by \(x^2 - 4\) while forgetting to include the \(+\frac{1}{2}x^3\) term in \(Q(x)\), which gives \(R_f(x) = 2x + 4\) and \(R_f(5) = 14\).
questions.explanation: We solve the problem in two key phases: identifying the polynomial \(f(x)\) from its graphical features, and applying the Polynomial Remainder Theorem to determine \(R(x)\). **Step 1: Determine \(f(x)\)** - Because the graph is tangent to the \(x\)-axis at \(x = -2\), \((x + 2)\) is a factor with an even multiplicity of at least \(2\). - Because the graph crosses the \(x\)-axis at \(x = 1\) and \(x = 3\), \((x - 1)\) and \((x - 3)\) are factors with odd multiplicities of at least \(1\). - Since \(f(x)\) is of degree 4, the sum of multiplicities must equal 4. Therefore, the multiplicity of \((x + 2)\) is 2, and the multiplicities of \((x - 1)\) and \((x - 3)\) are each 1: \(f(x) = a(x + 2)^2(x - 1)(x - 3)\) Using the \(y\)-intercept \((0, -6)\): \(f(0) = a(0 + 2)^2(0 - 1)(0 - 3) = a(4)(-1)(-3) = 12a = -6 \Rightarrow a = -\frac{1}{2}\) Thus, \(f(x) = -\frac{1}{2}(x + 2)^2(x - 1)(x - 3).\) **Step 2: Apply the Division Algorithm** When \(Q(x)\) is divided by the quadratic divisor \(x^2 - 4 = (x - 2)(x + 2)\), the remainder \(R(x)\) has degree at most 1, so \(R(x) = mx + b\). questions.q: The graph of a polynomial function \(f(x)\) is shown below. Which of the following could be the equation for \(f(x)\)?
questions.answer: To determine which polynomial function matches the graph, we analyze the intercepts, multiplicities, and end behavior: 1. **Identify the \(x\)-intercepts (zeros):** The graph crosses the \(x\)-axis at \(x = -2\), \(x = 1\), and \(x = 3\). By the Factor Theorem, if \(c\) is a zero of \(f(x)\), then \((x - c)\) is a factor. Therefore, the corresponding linear factors are: \((x - (-2)) = (x + 2), \quad (x - 1), \quad \mathrm{and} \quad (x - 3)\) 2. **Multiplicity:** At each of the three \(x\)-intercepts, the graph passes directly through the \(x\)-axis without flattening or turning around, indicating each zero has an odd multiplicity of \(1\). 3. **End Behavior and Leading Coefficient:** As \(x \rightarrow \infty\), \(f(x) \rightarrow \infty\), and as \(x \rightarrow -\infty\), \(f(x) \rightarrow -\infty\). This down-to-up end behavior is characteristic of an odd-degree polynomial with a positive leading coefficient. 4. **Check the \(y\)-intercept:** Evaluating \(f(0)\) for \(f(x) = (x + 2)(x - 1)(x - 3)\): \(f(0) = (0 + 2)(0 - 1)(0 - 3) = (2)(-1)(-3) = 6\) This matches the positive \(y\)-intercept visible on the graph. **Analysis of Distractors:** - Choice B confuses the zeros with their factors: it has zeros at \(x = 2, -1, -3\). - Choice C has a negative leading coefficient, which would cause \(f(x) \rightarrow -\infty\) as \(x \rightarrow \infty\) and give a negative \(y\)-intercept of \(-6\). - Choice D has a factor of \((x - 1)^2\), meaning the graph would touch and turn around at \(x = 1\) rather than cross the \(x\)-axis, and has an even degree of 4.

questions.q: The graph of the quadratic function \(f(x) = a(x - h)^2 + k\) is shown in the \(xy\)-plane with vertex \((2, 9)\) and \(y\)-intercept \((0, 5)\). A linear function is defined by \(g(x) = mx + 1\). If the graph of \(g\) passes through the vertex of the graph of \(f\), what is the other \(x\)-coordinate where the graphs of \(f\) and \(g\) intersect?
questions.target: Domain and range of composite and inverse functions
questions.answer: We solve the problem in three steps: 1. **Determine the quadratic function \(f(x)\):** The vertex is given as \((h, k) = (2, 9)\), so the function has the form: \(f(x) = a(x - 2)^2 + 9\) Since the graph passes through the point \((0, 5)\): $5 = a(0 - 2)^2 + 9 \Rightarrow 4a + 9 = 5 \Rightarrow 4a = -4 \Rightarrow a = -1\( Expanding \)f(x)\(: \)f(x) = -(x - 2)^2 + 9 = -(x^2 - 4x + 4) + 9 = -x^2 + 4x + 5\( 2. **Determine the linear function \)g(x)\(:** The line \)g(x) = mx + 1\( passes through the vertex \)(2, 9)\(: \)9 = m(2) + 1 \Rightarrow 2m = 8 \Rightarrow m = 4\( Thus, \)g(x) = 4x + 1\(. 3. **Find the points of intersection:** Set \)f(x) = g(x)\(: \)-x^2 + 4x + 5 = 4x + 1\( Subtract \)4x\( from both sides: \)-x^2 + 5 = 1 \Rightarrow -x^2 = -4 \Rightarrow x^2 = 4\( This yields \)x = 2\( and \)x = -2\(. Since \)x = 2\( corresponds to the given vertex, the other \)x\(-coordinate of intersection is \)-2$.

questions.q: The graph of the quadratic function \(f(x)\) is shown in the figure, with its vertex at \((1, 8)\) and an \(x\)-intercept at \((3, 0)\). A second function \(g\) is defined by \(g(x) = f(x - 2) + k\), where \(k\) is a constant. If the graph of \(g\) passes through the origin \((0, 0)\), what is the value of \(k\)?
questions.target: Applying composite and inverse functions in context
questions.answer: Step 1: Write the equation of \(f(x)\) in vertex form. Since the vertex is \((h, k_v) = (1, 8)\), the quadratic function has the form: \(f(x) = a(x - 1)^2 + 8\) Step 2: Use the known point \((3, 0)\) to solve for \(a\). \(f(3) = a(3 - 1)^2 + 8 = 0 \Rightarrow 4a + 8 = 0 \Rightarrow a = -2\) Thus, \(f(x) = -2(x - 1)^2 + 8\). Step 3: Apply the condition that \(g(x)\) passes through \((0, 0)\). \(g(0) = f(0 - 2) + k = 0 \Rightarrow f(-2) + k = 0\) Step 4: Evaluate \(f(-2)\). \(f(-2) = -2(-2 - 1)^2 + 8 = -2(-3)^2 + 8 = -2(9) + 8 = -10\) Step 5: Solve for \(k\). \(-10 + k = 0 \Rightarrow k = 10\) Common Misconceptions: - Evaluating \(f(2)\) instead of \(f(-2)\) yields \(f(2) = 6\), leading to \(k = -6\). - Confusing the value of \(f(-2) = -10\) directly with \(k\) leads to \(k = -10\).

questions.q: The quadratic function \(f(x) = ax^2 + bx + c\) is graphed in the standard \((x, y)\) coordinate plane below. The vertex of the parabola is at \((3, -6)\), and the graph passes through the point \((1, 2)\). What is the value of \(b\)?
questions.answer: 1. Write the quadratic function in vertex form: \(f(x) = a(x - h)^2 + k\). 2. Given the vertex \((h, k) = (3, -6)\), the function is \(f(x) = a(x - 3)^2 - 6\). 3. Use the given point \((1, 2)\) on the graph to find \(a\): $2 = a(1 - 3)^2 - 6\( \)2 = 4a - 6 \Rightarrow 4a = 8 \Rightarrow a = 2.\( 4. Expand the equation to standard form \)ax^2 + bx + c\(: \)f(x) = 2(x^2 - 6x + 9) - 6 = 2x^2 - 12x + 18 - 6 = 2x^2 - 12x + 12.\( 5. Comparing coefficients gives \)b = -12\(. Common error: A student who ignores the scale factor \)a\( might calculate \)b = -2h = -6\(, incorrectly choosing \)-6$.

questions.q: The function \(f(x) = a \cos(bx) + d\), where \(a, b,\) and \(d\) are positive constants, has a period of \(\pi\), a maximum value of \(7\), and satisfies \(f\left(\frac{\pi}{6}\right) = 4\). What is the value of \(f\left(\frac{\pi}{3}\right)\)?
questions.answer: We determine the unknown parameters \(a, b,\) and \(d\) step by step: 1. **Find \(b\) using the period:** The period of \(f(x) = a \cos(bx) + d\) is given by \(\frac{2\pi}{b}\). Setting this equal to \(\pi\): \(\frac{2\pi}{b} = \pi \Rightarrow b = 2\) 2. **Use the maximum value to relate \(a\) and \(d\):** Since \(a > 0\), the maximum value occurs when \(\cos(bx) = 1\): \(a(1) + d = 7 \Rightarrow a + d = 7\) 3. **Use the given point \(f\left(\frac{\pi}{6}\right) = 4\):** Substitute \(b = 2\) and \(x = \frac{\pi}{6}\): \(f\left(\frac{\pi}{6}\right) = a \cos\left(2 \cdot \frac{\pi}{6}\right) + d = a \cos\left(\frac{\pi}{3}\right) + d = 4\) Since \(\cos\left(\frac{\pi}{3}\right) = \frac{1}{2}\), this yields: \(\frac{1}{2}a + d = 4\) 4. **Solve the system of equations:** Subtracting the second equation from the first: \((a + d) - \left(\frac{1}{2}a + d\right) = 7 - 4 \Rightarrow \frac{1}{2}a = 3 \Rightarrow a = 6\) Then \(d = 7 - 6 = 1\). Thus, \(f(x) = 6 \cos(2x) + 1\). 5. **Evaluate \(f\left(\frac{\pi}{3}\right)\):** \(f\left(\frac{\pi}{3}\right) = 6 \cos\left(2 \cdot \frac{\pi}{3}\right) + 1 = 6 \cos\left(\frac{2\pi}{3}\right) + 1\) Since \(\frac{2\pi}{3}\) lies in Quadrant II, \(\cos\left(\frac{2\pi}{3}\right) = -\frac{1}{2}\): \(f\left(\frac{\pi}{3}\right) = 6\left(-\frac{1}{2}\right) + 1 = -3 + 1 = -2\) **Common Traps:** - Misidentifying \(\cos\left(\frac{2\pi}{3}\right)\) as \(+\frac{1}{2}\) gives \(6\left(\frac{1}{2}\right) + 1 = 4\). - Confusing the required evaluation with the vertical midline gives \(d = 1\). - Evaluating at the minimum of the sinusoid gives \(d - a = 1 - 6 = -5\).

questions.q: A function \(f\) is defined for all real numbers \(x\) such that \(x eq 0\) and \(x eq 1\). If \(f(x) + 2f\left(\frac{1}{1-x}\right) = 3x\) for all permissible values of \(x\), what is the value of \(f(3)\)?
questions.answer: To find \(f(3)\), we use the cyclic substitution property of the transformation \(T(x) = \frac{1}{1-x}\). 1. Substitute \(x = 3\) into the given functional equation: \(f(3) + 2f\left(\frac{1}{1-3}\right) = 3(3) \Rightarrow f(3) + 2f\left(-\frac{1}{2}\right) = 9 \quad \mathrm{---\ (Equation\ 1)}\) 2. Next, evaluate the equation at \(x = -\frac{1}{2}\): \(\frac{1}{1 - (-1/2)} = \frac{1}{3/2} = \frac{2}{3}\) \(f\left(-\frac{1}{2}\right) + 2f\left(\frac{2}{3}\right) = 3\left(-\frac{1}{2}\right) = -\frac{3}{2} \quad \mathrm{---\ (Equation\ 2)}\) 3. Now evaluate the equation at \(x = \frac{2}{3}\): \(\frac{1}{1 - 2/3} = \frac{1}{1/3} = 3\) \(f\left(\frac{2}{3}\right) + 2f(3) = 3\left(\frac{2}{3}\right) = 2 \quad \mathrm{---\ (Equation\ 3)}\) Let \(u = f(3)\), \(v = f\left(-\frac{1}{2}\right)\), and \(w = f\left(\frac{2}{3}\right)\). The system of linear equations is: 1) \(u + 2v = 9\) 2) \(v + 2w = -\frac{3}{2}\) 3) \(2u + w = 2 \Rightarrow w = 2 - 2u\) Substitute \(w\) into Equation 2: \(v + 2(2 - 2u) = -\frac{3}{2} \Rightarrow v + 4 - 4u = -\frac{3}{2} \Rightarrow v = 4u - \frac{11}{2}\) Substitute \(v\) into Equation 1: \(u + 2\left(4u - \frac{11}{2}\right) = 9\) \(u + 8u - 11 = 9\) \(9u = 20 \Rightarrow u = \frac{20}{9}\) Thus, \(f(3) = \frac{20}{9}\). A common misconception is assuming \(f(x) = x\), which would incorrectly yield \(3\). Another mistake is confusing the cyclic terms without systematically solving the 3-variable linear system.

questions.q: Which of the following statements describes the end behavior of the polynomial function \(f(x) = -5x^4 + 2x^3 - 7x + 3\)?
questions.answer: To determine the end behavior of a polynomial function, examine its leading term, which dominates the function's values for very large positive and negative values of \(x\). 1. Identify the leading term: The highest power of \(x\) is \(4\), so the leading term is \(-5x^4\). 2. Analyze the degree and leading coefficient: - The degree is \(n = 4\), which is an even integer. - The leading coefficient is \(a = -5\), which is negative. 3. Determine the limits as \(x \rightarrow \pm\infty\): - As \(x \rightarrow \infty\), \(x^4 \rightarrow \infty\), so \(-5x^4 \rightarrow -\infty\). Hence, \(f(x) \rightarrow -\infty\). - As \(x \rightarrow -\infty\), \(x^4 = (-|x|)^4 \rightarrow \infty\), so \(-5x^4 \rightarrow -\infty\). Hence, \(f(x) \rightarrow -\infty\). Therefore, the graph of \(f(x)\) falls to the left and falls to the right. Common Misconceptions: - Choice B confuses even-degree end behavior with odd-degree behavior having a negative leading coefficient (like \(y = -x^3\)). - Choice C corresponds to an odd degree with a positive leading coefficient (like \(y = x^3\)). - Choice D assumes that because the degree is even, both ends must go up to \(+\infty\), forgetting that the negative leading coefficient reflects the graph vertically.

questions.q: A factory produces two types of components, A and B, using two machines, M1 and M2. The time (in minutes) required to produce one unit of each component on each machine is given in the table below: | Component | Machine M1 | Machine M2 | |---|---|---| | A | 2 | 3 | | B | 4 | 1 | The factory has 480 minutes of M1 time and 240 minutes of M2 time available per day. Let \(x\) be the number of units of component A produced per day and \(y\) be the number of units of component B produced per day. Suppose the profit from selling one unit of component A is \(5\) and the profit from selling one unit of component B is \(8\). The factory wants to maximize its total daily profit. Formulate this problem as a linear programming problem, defining the objective function and the constraints.
questions.target: Applying composite and inverse functions in context
questions.answer: The objective is to maximize the total daily profit. The profit from selling \(x\) units of component A is \(5x\) and the profit from selling \(y\) units of component B is \(8y\). Therefore, the objective function is \(P = 5x + 8y\). The constraints are based on the available machine time. For Machine M1, producing \(x\) units of A takes \(2x\) minutes and producing \(y\) units of B takes \(4y\) minutes. The total time on M1 must be less than or equal to the available 480 minutes: \(2x + 4y \leq 480\). For Machine M2, producing \(x\) units of A takes \(3x\) minutes and producing \(y\) units of B takes \(y\) minutes. The total time on M2 must be less than or equal to the available 240 minutes: \(3x + y \leq 240\). Since the number of components produced cannot be negative, we have the non-negativity constraints: \(x \geq 0\) and \(y \geq 0\). Combining these, the linear programming problem is: Maximize \(P = 5x + 8y\) subject to \(2x + 4y \leq 480\), \(3x + y \leq 240\), \(x \geq 0\), \(y \geq 0\).

questions.q: The graph of the polynomial function \(f(x) = x^3 - ax^2 + bx - 6\) has a local maximum at \(x = -1\) and a local minimum at \(x = 3\). Determine the value of \(a+b\).
questions.answer: To find the local extrema of a polynomial function, we need to find its critical points by taking the derivative and setting it to zero. The derivative of \(f(x)\) is \(f'(x) = 3x^2 - 2ax + b\). Since \(f(x)\) has local extrema at \(x = -1\) and \(x = 3\), these are the roots of \(f'(x) = 0\). Thus, we can write \(f'(x)\) in factored form: \(f'(x) = k(x - (-1))(x - 3) = k(x+1)(x-3)\) for some constant \(k\). Expanding this, we get \(f'(x) = k(x^2 - 2x - 3)\). Comparing the coefficient of \(x^2\) in \(f'(x) = 3x^2 - 2ax + b\) and \(f'(x) = k(x^2 - 2x - 3)\), we see that \(k=3\). So, \(f'(x) = 3(x^2 - 2x - 3) = 3x^2 - 6x - 9\). Now, we can equate the coefficients of the two expressions for \(f'(x)\): \(-2ax = -6x\) implies \(2a = 6\), so \(a = 3\). \(b = -9\). Therefore, \(a+b = 3 + (-9) = -6\).
questions.explanation: To find the local extrema of a polynomial function, we need to find its critical points by taking the derivative and setting it to zero. The derivative of \(f(x)\) is \(f'(x) = 3x^2 - 2ax + b\). Since \(f(x)\) has local extrema at \(x = -1\) and \(x = 3\), these are the roots of \(f'(x) = 0\). Thus, we can write \(f'(x)\) in factored form: \(f'(x) = k(x - (-1))(x - 3) = k(x+1)(x-3)\) for some constant \(k\). Expanding this, we get \(f'(x) = k(x^2 - 2x - 3)\). Comparing the coefficient of \(x^2\) in \(f'(x) = 3x^2 - 2ax + b\) and \(f'(x) = k(x^2 - 2x - 3)\), we see that \(k=3\). So, \(f'(x) = 3(x^2 - 2x - 3) = 3x^2 - 6x - 9\). Now, we can equate the coefficients of the two expressions for \(f'(x)\): \(-2ax = -6x\) implies \(2a = 6\), so \(a = 3\). \(b = -9\). Therefore, \(a+b = 3 + (-9) = -6\).

questions.q: Convert \(360°\) to radians.
questions.answer: **Answer:** C. \(360°\times\dfrac{\pi}{180°}=2\pi.\)
